title: Area X review: Postflight Procedures
intro: Area X has one Task, checking instruments and equipment after flight, and it only matters because of what happened in the flight before it. These questions join it to the other Areas: a real vacuum failure on an instrument proficiency check, a frozen static system on an ILS, a dual VOR check on a tracking lesson, P-static in snow, a glideslope flag, a GPS outage in a testing area, a deferred DME, an encoder repair, closing the flight plan after practice approaches, a radio failure before an IMC trip, and the debrief and records check that tie one lesson to the next.

questions.q: During an instrument proficiency check in actual IMC, your client's vacuum pump really fails, and he flies the approach partial panel to a safe landing. He owns the airplane, which has no MEL. He wants to placard the attitude and heading indicators INOPERATIVE, fly home IFR tomorrow, and fix them at the annual next month. What do you tell him?
options: He may, if a mechanic deactivates them and a rated pilot finds they are no hazard under 91.213(d)
He may, since an owner can leave any placarded item until the next required inspection
Not IFR: 91.205(d) requires both, so they need repair and a return-to-service entry first
Not IFR until he gets an MEL, since without one, 91.213(d) deferrals cover VFR flights only
questions.why: For IFR flight, 91.205(d) requires a gyroscopic pitch and bank indicator and a gyroscopic direction indicator [[60:488|14 CFR 91.205(d)]], and 91.213(d) cannot be used for an item required by 91.205 for the kind of flight operation being conducted [[60:493|14 CFR 91.213(d)(2)(iii)]]. An MEL would not help either: instruments required for specific operations by Part 91 may not be included in one [[60:492|14 CFR 91.213(b)(3)]]. Waiting for the next required inspection applies only to items permitted to be inoperative by 91.213(d)(2) [[60:521|14 CFR 91.405(c)]]; other discrepancies are repaired between inspections [[60:520|14 CFR 91.405(a)]], and after the repair no one may operate the airplane until it is approved for return to service and the entry is made [[60:521|14 CFR 91.407(a)]]. In flight, the IFH has the pilot advise ATC of an instrument failure and declare an emergency if necessary [[23:332|IFH 11-7]].

questions.q: On a practice ILS in heavy rain, your learner's airspeed indicator, altimeter and VSI all freeze. She selects the alternate static source and the indications come back. After landing, a mechanic drains water from the static system through its drain only, then closes it. Before the next IFR flight in controlled airspace, what does 91.411 require?
options: A new static test, because selecting the alternate source opened the static system
Only a check flight logged by a private pilot before anyone else rides along
A new static and altimeter test, because water in the lines voids the last test
No new test for using the drain and alternate static valve; the 24-month test still applies
questions.why: After any opening and closing of the static pressure system, 91.411 requires a new test before IFR in controlled airspace, except for the use of the system drain and alternate static pressure valves [[60:524|14 CFR 91.411(a)(2)]]. The test of the static system, altimeter and altitude reporting within the preceding 24 calendar months still applies [[60:524|14 CFR 91.411(a)(1)]]. A static system problem affects the ASI, altimeter and VSI together, and most aircraft have an alternate static source the pilot can select [[23:333|IFH 11-8]]. The 91.407(b) check flight is for maintenance that may have appreciably changed flight characteristics or substantially affected operation in flight [[60:521|14 CFR 91.407(b)]]; it is not part of 91.411. Application: the write-up still matters, so maintenance can find how the water got in.

questions.q: On a tracking lesson (VII.A), your learner tunes both VOR receivers to the same station and centers each CDI: NAV 1 shows 093° TO and NAV 2 shows 098° TO. She wants to log it as her 30-day VOR check. What do you teach?
options: It passes: 5° is inside the 6° allowed for any VOR check made in the air
It fails: two receivers checked against each other may differ by 4° at most
It does not count: a dual check is valid only on the ground before departure
It passes if she logs the average of the two bearings as the bearing error
questions.why: With a dual VOR system, one system may be checked against the other in place of the 91.171(b) checks: both are tuned to the same facility, and the maximum permissible variation between the two indicated bearings is 4 degrees [[60:471|14 CFR 91.171(c)]], so 5° fails, and 91.171(c) does not say the check must be on the ground. The 6° limit belongs to the airborne checks against a designated airborne checkpoint or a ground point on an airway radial [[60:470|14 CFR 91.171(b)(3)]] [[60:471|14 CFR 91.171(b)(4)(iii)]]. Without a valid check within the preceding 30 days, the VOR may not be used under IFR [[60:470|14 CFR 91.171(a)(2)]]. Whoever makes a check enters the date, place and bearing error and signs the aircraft log or other record [[60:471|14 CFR 91.171(d)]]; a failed check is also a squawk for maintenance.

questions.q: On an IFR cross-country through steady snow, your learner's headset fills with a high-pitched squeal, VHF reception fades on both radios, and the magnetic compass swings. Everything clears up soon after the snow ends. After landing, what do you have her check and write up?
options: The static wicks: replace any broken or missing ones before an instrument flight
Both com radios: two fading together in snow points to a fault inside the radios only
Nothing: the symptoms ended with the snow, so there is no equipment problem to record
The compass alone: static in snow magnetizes it, so it must be swung before flying again
questions.why: Precipitation static builds with time as the airplane flies in rain or snow, and can cause erroneous magnetic compass readings, complete loss of VHF communications and high-pitched audio squealing. To reduce it, the pilot should make sure the static wicks are properly maintained and accounted for, and broken or missing wicks should be replaced before an instrument flight [[23:328|IFH 11-3]]. So the symptoms ending with the snow fits P-static, but it does not show the wicks are intact. Poor quality communications reception is also on the AIM's list of problems worth reporting [[33:87|AIM 1-1-13]]. No source here says static magnetizes a compass.

questions.q: Under IFR in controlled airspace, the glideslope flag on your learner's receiver drops into view halfway down a practice ILS (VIII.B), while the localizer stays good. She continues to the localizer minimums without saying anything to ATC and lands. What did she owe?
options: Nothing: the localizer still worked, and only a complete ILS loss must be reported
A GPS Anomaly Reporting Form after landing, which covers ILS receivers too
A squawk only: 91.187 covers failures that end an approach, not partial ones
A report to ATC as soon as practical, and a written squawk for maintenance after landing
questions.why: Under IFR in controlled airspace, the pilot in command must report to ATC as soon as practical any malfunction of navigation, approach or communication equipment occurring in flight, giving identification, equipment affected, degree of impairment and assistance desired [[60:483|14 CFR 91.187]]. The AIM lists complete or partial loss of ILS receiver capability among the reports made without an ATC request [[33:377|AIM 5-3-3]]. The GPS Anomaly Reporting Form is for GPS problems [[33:88|AIM 1-1-13]]. The radio call does not reach maintenance: after the flight, squawks and discrepancies should be noted and reported to maintenance [[24:349|AFH 17-15]], in the maintenance or discrepancy record provided for that purpose [[1:240|PHAK 9-10]].

questions.q: On an RNAV (GPS) approach lesson (VIII.A), your learner's GPS loses integrity inside the area of a published GPS testing NOTAM. Nothing else fails, and she asks for the VOR approach instead. What should she tell ATC in flight, and what follows after landing?
options: Only what she needs for an amended clearance; the details can go on the FAA form after the flight
A full anomaly report in flight, with position, altitude and duration, since 91.187 has no exceptions
Nothing in flight or after: anomalies inside a NOTAMed test area are never reported in any form
Nothing in flight; after landing she phones the test range, which passes the report to ATC for her
questions.why: To minimize ATC workload, GPS anomalies associated with known testing NOTAMs should not be reported to ATC in flight in detail, except when the degradation is outside the NOTAMed area or the pilot sees unexpected consequences such as equipment failure or suspected spoofing [[33:88|AIM 1-1-13]]. A pilot who meets a navigation error should transition to another navigation source and request amended clearances as necessary [[33:87|AIM 1-1-13]]. GPS problems should also be reported after the flight on the FAA GPS Anomaly Reporting Form [[33:88|AIM 1-1-13]], so "never reported in any form" goes too far. No source here mentions phoning a test range.

questions.q: No MEL. After a DME arc lesson (VII.A), the club's DME receiver is found dead. A mechanic deactivates it and records the work, it is placarded INOPERATIVE, and he finds it is no hazard. Nothing in the type certification, equipment list, KOEL, ADs or the club's IFR flights requires it, and the next arc lesson will use the IFR GPS. When must the owner have the DME repaired?
options: At the next required inspection, since 91.213(d)(2) allowed it to be inoperative
Within 30 days, matching the interval 91.171 sets for the VOR check
Before any further IFR flight, since all IFR navigation equipment must work
Never, as long as the GPS can stand in for it on every arc and every DME fix
questions.why: The owner must have any inoperative instrument or item permitted to be inoperative by 91.213(d)(2) repaired, replaced, removed or inspected at the next required inspection [[60:521|14 CFR 91.405(c)]]. The deferral itself needs the 91.213(d) conditions: the item deactivated and placarded, any deactivation that involves maintenance done and recorded under Part 43, and a determination that it is no hazard [[60:493|14 CFR 91.213(d)]]. For IFR, 91.205(d) asks for navigation equipment suitable for the route, not every receiver installed [[60:488|14 CFR 91.205(d)]], and DME or a suitable RNAV system becomes required only at and above FL 240 when VOR is required [[60:488|14 CFR 91.205(e)]]. IFR-certified GPS may be substituted for DME when flying a DME arc [[23:301|IFH 10-10]], but that does not cancel the owner's repair duty.

questions.q: En route on an IFR training flight, ATC tells your learner that her Mode C altitude does not agree with the altitude she reported. After the flight, an avionics shop repairs the altitude encoder and approves it for return to service. Before the next IFR flight in controlled airspace, what else must be done?
options: Nothing more: the return-to-service entry covers it, and the 24-month test stays valid
A test of the integrated system, since the work could cause a data correspondence error
A static system test only, since the shop's sign-off already approves the encoder itself
An operational check flight with no passengers aboard, logged in the aircraft records
questions.why: After installation or maintenance on the transponder's automatic pressure altitude reporting system where a data correspondence error could be introduced, the integrated system must be tested, inspected and found to comply before IFR in controlled airspace [[60:524|14 CFR 91.411(a)(3)]]; 91.413 says the same for that kind of work on the transponder [[60:525|14 CFR 91.413(b)]]. The return-to-service entry is required [[60:521|14 CFR 91.407(a)]] but does not replace that test. The 91.407(b) check flight applies to maintenance that may have appreciably changed flight characteristics or substantially affected operation in flight [[60:521|14 CFR 91.407(b)]].

questions.q: After practice approaches, your learner lands on her IFR flight plan at a nontowered field with no FSS. On the ramp her radio cannot reach ATC, and she says the flight plan will close itself, the way it did at the towered airport last week. What do you teach?
options: It closes on landing at any airport, towered or not, once she sets the transponder to standby
She does nothing now and cancels it on her next flight, while airborne and in radio contact
It closes by itself half an hour after her ETA, when search and rescue calls the field
She must cancel it now by telephone, and next time cancel in the air if she can finish VFR
questions.why: An IFR flight plan closes automatically on landing only at an airport with an operating control tower; at a nontowered airport the pilot is responsible for canceling it, by telephone after landing if there is no operating FSS or other direct way to reach ATC [[23:294|IFH 10-3]] [[33:340|AIM 5-1-15]]. Where ATC cannot be reached on the ground, the pilot may cancel while still airborne and able to talk to ATC, if the rest of the flight can be VFR [[23:294|IFH 10-3]], which quickly releases the airspace for other aircraft [[33:340|AIM 5-1-15]]. The half-hour search and rescue rule is written for VFR and DVFR flight plans [[33:339|AIM 5-1-14]]. The rule itself: on canceling or completing the flight, the pilot in command notifies an FSS or ATC facility [[60:470|14 CFR 91.169(d)]].

questions.q: After a partial panel approach lesson (IX.B), your learner replays the flight and says she caught the vacuum failure right away. Your written notes show two minutes on the failed attitude indicator before she noticed. In the four-step debrief, what do you do with that?
options: Let it go: in the replay step you only listen, and corrections wait for your own grading
Skip ahead to redirect and tell her how to scan, since the replay step is for praise only
Discuss the mismatch at the right moment, since her replay shows how she judges herself
Accept her account, since in collaborative assessment the learner's own view comes first
questions.why: In the replay step the instructor listens for areas where the learner's account does not seem accurate and, at the right moment, discusses the discrepancy with her; this lets her validate her own perceptions and gives you insight into her judgment [[25:136|AIH 6-5]]. Postflight critiques in written notes help you cover all the areas you noticed [[25:182|AIH 9-12]]. Self-assessment comes first in collaborative assessment, but it is followed by a discussion that compares your assessment with hers [[25:182|AIH 9-12]]. The scan point to reconstruct: a failure usually shows as a warning indicator or as the attitude indicator disagreeing with the supporting instruments [[23:332|IFH 11-7]].

questions.q: COM 2 failed on today's lesson and has been properly deferred under 91.213(d). Tomorrow your learner plans a single-pilot IFR trip in forecast IMC with COM 1 working. She asks whether that is a problem, since the airplane is legal. What do you teach?
options: No problem: once a deferral is legal, the RMH treats the item as no longer a hazard
Legal is not the end: in IMC the RMH calls a single radio a possible "A" hazard
It is illegal: a deferred radio may not be flown in IMC until it has been repaired
It matters only at night, the one time the RMH says radio redundancy is a concern
questions.why: The RMH says a single nav/com radio is not a major concern on a day VFR flight in Class E airspace, but for a flight in IMC one radio could be considered an "A" hazard, and instrument failure is a concern in IMC or at night [[30:24|RMH 3-6]]. Inoperative equipment triggers an "A" hazard, and the pilot weighs its effect against the expected flight conditions [[30:25|RMH 3-7]]. A proper 91.213(d) deferral makes the takeoff legal [[60:493|14 CFR 91.213(d)]], and the item waits for the next required inspection [[60:521|14 CFR 91.405(c)]]; neither rule adds an IMC limit. The PHAK also warns that deferral is not to be taken lightly, particularly when other items are inoperative [[1:240|PHAK 9-10]].

questions.q: Your morning learner squawked a flickering NAV 1 flag on the club airplane. Your afternoon learner, booked for a holding lesson (VII.B) in the same airplane, wants to skip the paperwork and start the preflight right away. What does the AIH say you should do first?
options: Preflight first, and read the squawk sheet only if something looks wrong on the walkaround
Leave the records to the club, since checking them is the renter's job and not the instructor's
Check the airplane's airworthiness status and review the discrepancy report, with her involved
Ask the morning learner if the flag still flickered at the end, and go if she says it cleared
questions.why: The AIH says the instructor should determine the aircraft's official airworthiness status before scheduled flights and before the preflight, know the operator's procedures for reporting and correcting discrepancies, review the current discrepancy report, resolve questions with maintenance before the preflight inspection, and consider involving the learner [[25:191|AIH 10-7]]. The AFH has the pilot inspect the logbooks or a summary of the airworthy status before flight [[24:39|AFH 2-2]], and any discrepancies need to be addressed prior to flight [[24:41|AFH 2-4]]. The pilot in command decides whether the airplane is in condition for safe flight [[60:436|14 CFR 91.7(b)]], and involving the learner shows her that this check manages the risk of failed equipment [[25:191|AIH 10-7]].
